title: Leaning Poles
logline: A crew raises a tall bamboo frame for a village festival, poles leaning against each other's tips until, all at once, the structure holds on its own, decorations hanging from a frame that itself stands only because nothing in it stands alone.

object.note: Object 9 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: Split vine woven into something no single length could make leads to bamboo poles leaning on each other's tips until, together, the frame holds.

thread_out.thread: A festival frame that stands only because nothing in it stands alone becomes a roof renewed leaf by leaf, still 'the same roof' each year, an echo of 'The Same Boat'.

requirements: A village crew building a festival structure from raw materials on site, not pre-fabricated
A fixed opening date to build toward
Safe filming positions during the raising

suggestions.name: A village temple ground during a local festival season
suggestions.why: Deliberately a smaller, local festival rather than a major national procession, to allow closer access to one crew's whole build.
suggestions.verify: A specific festival, crew and structure must be found and confirmed.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed.

lesson.in_simple_terms: The festival frame stands only because its poles lean on each other. But the texts are careful: not everything that stands together holds everything else up.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: සමහර දේ නැගී සිටින්නේ කණු මෙන් එකිනෙකට හේත්තු වීමෙන් පමණක් වුවත්, එකට තිබෙන සෑම දෙයක්ම අනෙක් සෑම දෙයකටම පිහිට වන්නේ නැත.
lesson.the_teaching: The Paṭṭhāna's mutuality condition (aññamañña) is support that runs both ways between things that arise together, like several sticks that stay upright only by leaning on each other's tips. The text immediately adds a limit: mind supports the matter it gives rise to, but that matter does not support the mind in return. In the texts' summary, mutual support is only one of nine ways mind and matter hold each other up.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: Poles are chosen and lashed, a first attempt fails and is corrected, and then comes the moment the frame holds with no hands on it; a pole is tested and the whole frame gives and recovers. Then decorations and lights are hung from a frame they do not hold up, so the viewer sees support that runs both ways beside support that runs only one way.

key_terms.en: co-arising: things that arise together supporting each other's arising
condition-power; the specific way one thing helps another

lesson.caution: Mutuality is not a picture of community cooperation or of 'everything supports everything': in the texts it describes states within a single moment of experience, and the frame is only an everyday image of it.
lesson.builds_on: The vine showed a chain that can be entered anywhere; the leaning poles show a different kind of support, running both ways at once between things that stand together.
